extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists and entrants to international cartoon/satire competitions; festival organizers and jurors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation dimensions used by international cartoon festivals and exhibitions to judge submitted cartoons, caricatures, gag/editorial cartoons, comics and related media. Covers thematic fit, artistic/technical quality, originality, social/political impact, category suitability, and procedural precautions (e.g., plagiarism checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to the theme / hitting the target theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Many competitions judge whether the artwork addresses the announced theme (e.g., “THE TIME IS RUNNING OUT”, “SILENCE”, “Tourism”, “Corruption”). Winners are noted for “getting the theme” or “hitting the target theme”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries reward works that respond directly and inventively to the competition theme — examples: “for getting the theme in a striking and hilarious humorous form”, “for hitting the target theme with an intensely poetical image”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic and technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of drawing/visual technique, composition, use of media and overall craftsmanship (referred to with phrases like “graphic sign”, “great skill of illustrator”, “technique”, “professional fulfillment”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries look for high-level execution: “wise and expressive graphic sign”, “great skill of illustrator”, “technique and dynamism of the script”, and award separate prizes for technical achievement in categories (video, comics, caricature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel or nontraditional approaches are valued (page notes juries considering “a nontraditional view of the issue” and organizers saying they “try to force the cartoonist to be creative”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality in concept, composition or approach increases chances: “originality to express the theme”, selecting themes that are ‘not so evident’ to encourage creative responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness / visual sign and synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to convey idea efficiently through a strong, expressive visual sign and graphic synthesis (phrases used: “graphic synthesis”, “expressive maturity”, “wise and expressive graphic sign”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that achieve a refined, concentrated visual statement — concise symbolism and synthesis — are singled out: “for the graphic synthesis, the refined message, the originality to express the theme.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor, irony and provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the work uses humor and irony effectively, including provocation as a device (explicitly: “That is one of the keys to irony, a provocation on his part.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries reward a strong ironic stance or provocative twist that serves the message; exaggeration and provocation are identified as comedic elements when used purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative, evocative quality and storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons are assessed for narrative content or evocative flavour — works may be praised for having a narrative or evocative quality beyond a single gag (“narrative and evocative flavour”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries that tell a mini-story or evoke a scene/feeling (diptychs, sequences, or single images with narrative depth) can be preferred in certain prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message clarity and refined message
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and sophistication of the intended message are evaluated — juries cite “refined message” as a reason for awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, focused message that is communicated with subtlety and refinement is rewarded, rather than muddled or ambiguous commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social / political relevance and criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are judged for topicality and for acting as critical commentary on social/political issues (“situating ourselves in the present time, ... exposing risks, lies and falsifications”, cartoons as exercise of freedom for the press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons that thoughtfully engage current events, politics or social problems and offer critical perspective are highly valued; editorial/cartoon categories emphasize this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category suitability (cartoon, gag, editorial, caricature, comic, video)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries must fit the submitted category (Cartoon, Satire & Humor, Caricature, Gag Cartoon, Editorial Cartoon, Video, Comic etc.) — different categories have different evaluation emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers separate prizes by category and expect works to conform to category norms (e.g., editorial cartoons for press-critical commentary; caricature for psychological interpretation; gag cartoons for single-panel humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological interpretation in personal caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: For caricature categories, judges value the artist’s capacity for psychological interpretation of the sitter/personality (“capacity for psychological interpretation in personal caricature”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caricature prizes reward insight into character/psychology and skillful exaggeration that reveals rather than merely distorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor and powerful imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective metaphors and potent visual metaphors (example: wall becomes a guillotine) are used as criteria for impact and creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphorical transformations that crystallize a complex idea into a single striking image are frequently rewarded and cited when explaining awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration as a deliberate device
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposeful exaggeration (of features, situations) is recognized as a comedic and critical tool (“exaggeration is the element of comedy”, “maximum exaggeration of the face”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration should serve insight or humor; juries praise maximum exaggeration when it enhances meaning rather than merely shocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical sensitivity / avoiding exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries and commentaries note ethical considerations — e.g., criticism of works that exploit tragedy as spectacle (“travel agencies that promote visits to slums, to witness misery, exploring local tragedy as an exotic setting”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists are implicitly expected to balance satire with ethical awareness; insensitive exploitation of suffering may be criticized even if visually striking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to provoke reflection / stimulate thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons are valued for stimulating reflection and debate rather than merely providing a quick laugh (“it aims to stimulate people to reflection ... stimulate people to reflection”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that prompt viewers to think, question or reconsider topics are seen as culturally valuable and often favored by juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience appeal / popularity (audience prizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some awards are decided by the audience — “Audience award”, “Audience Prizes” — reflecting public appeal separate from juried assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries that connect with visitors and the public (clear, emotionally resonant or immediately funny images) can win popular prizes even if juries select differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nontraditional perspective / innovative viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries explicitly reward nontraditional or unexpected perspectives on the subject (“nontraditional view of the issue”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaching a theme from an unusual angle or offering a surprising conceptual flip increases competitiveness, as seen in juries’ rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category-specific technical/format quality (video, comic strip, diptych)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media categories have specialized expectations — e.g., video judged for professional fulfillment, comics for dynamism of script, diptychs for narrative interplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers single out technical and narrative execution appropriate to the medium (e.g., video: professional fulfillment and thematic hitting; comic: technique and dynamism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / originality checks and pre-selection transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers take procedural steps to avoid awarding duplicated or plagiarized works (e.g., Olive Cartoon Contest publishes pre-selected works and asks the public to report similarities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions may publicly list pre-selected cartoons to detect plagiarized or duplicate work; entrants should avoid submitting previously published or substantially similar pieces and be prepared to document originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic maturity and expressive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of an author’s mature, consistent expressive voice or expressive maturity (e.g., “expressive maturity”, “creative design to which he has accustomed us”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries sometimes reward an artist’s established expressive strengths — consistent, mature stylistic voice and sustained conceptual depth can influence awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for formal contest rules and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: While not elaborated in detail on this page, multiple competitions imply adherence to organizational procedures (submission categories, exhibition rules, timelines, preselection lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrants must follow contest rules (themes, deadlines, category specifications); organizers may disqualify or publicize pre-selection to ensure fair judging.
